newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian edible oil trade seeks duty change, futures.
newsitem.headline: Indian edible oil trade seeks duty change, futures.

text.p: India's edible oil trade on Thursday urged the government to impose a seasonal duty structure on edible oil imports, or start futures trading to prevent a dip in prices and stabilise the market.
"The government should take steps and impose a variable duty structure on edible oil imports," O.P. Goenka, a senior official at the Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade, told Reuters.

Goenka said that during the season, the government should increase import duties on edible oils once domestic prices start falling on higher imports. The government could reduce it after prices firm up, he said.
Industry officials said palm olein prices had fallen to about 25,500 rupees per tonne from about 27,500 rupees in the past month.
Malaysian palm oil prices had eased during the period on expectations of a better crop.
"The international prices have gone down because Malaysia's palm oil crop is expected to be higher," Goenka said.

Traders in Malaysia said on Thursday that palm oil prices rose at midday following weakness in the ringgit against the U.S. dollar and expectations of good July 1-25 exports. The weaker ringgit makes it less expensive to buy Malaysian palm oil.
At midday, the Malaysian October contract was up eight ringgit at 1,162 ringgit ($437.02) a tonne.
Industry officials said about 35,000 tonnes of imported edible oil, comprising mainly palm olein from Malaysia and sunflower oil from South America, were arriving at Indian ports every week.

B.V. Mehta, executive director of the Solvent Extractors' Association of India, told Reuters that imports in 1996/97 (Nov-Oct) were expected to rise to about 1.6 million tonnes from 1.25 million tonnes last season.
"But the shortfall is only about 800,000 tonnes," Mehta said. "Therefore, there is a general glut in the market."
India imported about 900,000 tonnes of edible oil between November 1996 and June 1997. In 1995/96, the country imported 1.25 million tonnes of edible oil.

"When we have opened the floodgates to the world market, we should have futures trading in edible oil which should provide some kind of hedging," Navinbhai Shah, president of the Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, told Reuters.
"Then everybody involved in the trade can plan buying and selling properly."
Shah said that importers had booked heavily from Malaysia hoping that domestic market prices would rise, but excessive imports had flooded the market leading to a sharp price fall.
Industry officials said groundnut oil prices rose in the local markets following reports of deficient monsoon rains in the major groundnut growing regions.
"Rainfall in Saurashtra is not favourable," Mehta said. Saurashtra region in the western state of Gujarat accounts for 35 percent of the country's groundnut output.
"In addition, there are no imports of groundnut oil," Shah said. "Therefore, groundnut oil prices are rising."
Traders said groundnut oil was currently quoted at 38,000 rupees per tonne in the domestic market, up from 37,000 rupees last week.
